title: Elastic anomalies enabled by lattice distortion in high entropy alloys
abstract: Abstract Elastic anomalies, such as the Elinvar effect, large recoverable elastic strain, and nonlinear superelasticity, offer significant potential for engineering applications. High entropy alloys (HEAs) have recently emerged as a model system for investigating such unconventional elastic behaviors. In this Perspective, we review recent advances regarding lattice distortion enabled elastic anomalies in HEAs. We elucidate the origin of the Elinvar effect, where heterogeneous lattice strain fields counteract thermoelastic softening and stabilize elastic moduli over a broad temperature range. Furthermore, we discuss non-hysteretic superelasticity arising from severe lattice distortion, achieving a large elastic strain limit of ~ 2% with minimal energy dissipation. Finally, we address the transition from Hookean to non-Hookean superelasticity through the framework of distortion regulated martensitic transformation. Collectively, this work demonstrates that lattice distortion serves as a critical structural mechanism for tailoring elastic responses and guiding the design of advanced superelastic materials.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Elastic properties, encompassing both the elastic modulus and the elastic strain limit, are among the most fundamental physical characteristics of structural and functional materials [ 1 ,  2 ]. The elastic modulus determines a material’s stiffness and resistance to deformation, while the elastic strain limit defines the range of recoverable deformation before permanent plastic deformation is activated. Traditionally, the elastic behavior of crystalline metals is governed by stretching and shearing of atomic bonds, typically following Hooke’s law with an elastic limit of less than 1% [ 3 ,  4 ]. Conventional metals also suffer from significant modulus softening as temperature increases, as thermal vibrations weaken atomic bonds [ 5 ]. However, in advanced industries such as aerospace, precision instrumentation, and biomedical engineering, there are increasing demands for ultraelastic materials that exhibit high strength, large elastic strain, as well as the Elinvar effect, where the elastic modulus remains insensitive to temperature fluctuations [ 6 ,  7 – 8 ].

Among these phenomena, the Elinvar effect has attracted sustained attention due to its critical importance in applications requiring thermal stability and precision [ 6 ,  9  ]. Despite more than a century of research, the physical origins of the Elinvar effect remain complex, involving competing contributions from electronic or magnetic interactions, phase transitions, and lattice anharmonicity [ 10 ,  11 – 12 ]. Recent studies suggest that lattice distortion itself can serve as an independent mechanism to generate an additional elastic contribution that compensates thermoelastic softening, thereby stabilizing the elastic modulus across a wide temperature range [ 13 ,  14 ]. This emerging finding highlights the critical role of local structural heterogeneity in governing macroscopic elastic responses [ 13 ,  15 ]. In addition, the development of materials exhibiting large recoverable elastic strain has redefined the conventional limits of elastic behavior [ 16 ,  17 ]. Shape memory alloys (SMAs), strain glass alloys, and Gum metals can achieve superelastic strains exceeding several percent through stress-induced martensitic transformations or nanoscale structural rearrangements [ 18 ,  19 ,  20 – 21 ]. Nevertheless, such pseudoelasticity is often accompanied by mechanical hysteresis and energy dissipation, which limits their efficiency and reversibility [ 18 ]. The realization of non-hysteretic superelasticity remains a key challenge in this field.

The emergence of high entropy alloys (HEAs), composed of multiple principal elements with significant atomic size mismatch and chemical complexity, provides a unique platform to address these challenges [ 22 ,  23 – 24 ]. The inherent chemical disorder in HEAs introduces pronounced lattice distortion and heterogeneous strain fields at the atomic scale, which fundamentally alter phase stability, transformation pathways, and elastic behavior [ 25 ,  26 – 27 ]. Unlike conventional alloys, HEAs have been shown to exhibit a remarkable spectrum of elastic phenomena, including temperature independent elastic modulus, ultralarge elastic strain limits, and tunable transitions between Hookean and non-Hookean superelasticity [ 13 ,  28 ]. Recent breakthroughs demonstrate that lattice distortion in HEAs can generate a heterogeneous strain landscape, giving rise to unconventional elastic responses such as non-hysteretic superelasticity and reversible transitions between different elastic regimes [ 13 ,  28 ,  29 ]. Furthermore, the interplay between lattice distortion and martensitic transformation enables tuning of phase stability, allowing for the suppression, frustration, or activation of transformation pathways [ 28 ].

Although several reviews have discussed the mechanical behavior [ 30 ,  31 ], alloy design strategies [ 32 ] of HEAs and related complex alloys, most existing studies have primarily focused on strengthening mechanisms, phase stability, or conventional transformation-induced deformation behavior. In contrast, the role of lattice distortion as a fundamental structural parameter governing unconventional elastic responses remains insufficiently explored. Here, we aim to establish a unified framework linking atomic-scale lattice distortion with diverse elastic anomalies, including the Elinvar effect, non-hysteretic superelasticity, and the transition from Hookean to non-Hookean elasticity. This Perspective provides new insights into the structure–property relationships in chemically complex alloys and highlights lattice distortion engineering as a promising strategy for designing advanced ultraelastic materials. We systematically summarize recent progress on elastic anomalies enabled by lattice distortion in HEAs. We begin by elucidating the origin and underlying mechanisms of the Elinvar effect in highly distorted HEAs. Subsequently, we examine non-hysteretic superelasticity induced by heterogeneous strain fields, followed by a discussion of transformation-induced superelasticity associated with martensitic transitions. Finally, we analyze the role of lattice distortion in mediating the transition from linear to nonlinear elasticity and propose future research directions, thereby highlighting new opportunities for designing materials with programmable elastic responses.

sections.heading: Elinvar effect in distorted high entropy alloys
paragraphs: The Elinvar effect, characterized by a nearly temperature-independent elastic modulus over a broad temperature range, represents one of the most intriguing elastic anomalies in metallic materials [ 12 ,  33 ]. In conventional crystalline alloys, the elastic modulus generally decreases with increasing temperature because thermal vibrations weaken interatomic bonding and enhance lattice anharmonicity [ 5 ,  34 ,  35 ]. According to classical thermoelastic theory, thermal expansion increases the average atomic spacing and reduces the curvature of the interatomic potential well, resulting in modulus softening [ 35 ,  36 ]. Therefore, achieving a stable elastic modulus requires an additional hardening mechanism capable of compensating for the intrinsic thermoelastic softening.

Traditionally, the Elinvar effect has mainly been achieved through magnetoelastic coupling or phase transformation mechanisms [ 10 ,  11 ,  37 ,  20 ]. Classical FeNiCr-based Elinvar alloys rely on magnetic ordering to generate modulus hardening that offsets thermal softening [ 11 ,  38 ,  39 ]. Similarly, metastable alloys undergoing martensitic transformations, such as B2 to B19’ transitions, can exhibit Elinvar-like behavior due to transformation-related elastic anomalies and dynamic phase coexistence [ 18 ,  40 ,  41 ]. However, these conventional mechanisms often suffer from limited operational temperature windows, pronounced hysteresis, and poor reversibility because of the instability of magnetic domains or martensitic interfaces [ 42 ]. Consequently, developing structurally stable Elinvar materials independent of magnetic transitions or long-range martensitic transformations remains an important challenge.

Recent studies demonstrate that severe lattice distortion in HEAs and multi-principal element alloys provides a fundamentally different pathway for realizing the Elinvar effect [ 13 ,  15 ]. Owing to the coexistence of multiple principal elements with significant atomic size mismatch and chemical complexity, HEAs inherently possess pronounced local lattice distortion and heterogeneous strain fields at the atomic scale [ 25 ,  26  ]. Unlike conventional dilute alloys, where distortion is localized around isolated solute atoms, the distortion in HEAs is spatially pervasive and intrinsically coupled with local chemical and electronic heterogeneity [ 43 ,  44 – 45 ]. Such structural disorder fundamentally modifies the elastic response of the lattice and alters the temperature dependence of the elastic modulus. Experimentally, lattice distortion in HEAs can be characterized using diffraction and microscopy-based techniques, including X-ray or neutron diffraction peak broadening analysis [ 46 ,  47  ], pair distribution function (PDF) measurements [ 48 ], and atomic resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) combined with geometric phase analysis [ 49 ]. These methods enable quantitative mapping of local atomic displacement and strain heterogeneity beyond the average crystallographic structure. To further quantify distortion, atomistic simulations such as density functional theory (DFT) and ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) are widely employed to evaluate descriptors including volumetric strain, local bond length distribution, and von Mises strain, which provide statistical measures of local structural disorder and elastic energy landscapes [ 25 ,  50 ,  51  –]. For example, He et al. reported that the B2-structured Co 25 Ni 25 (TiZrHf) 50  high entropy intermetallic exhibits a pronounced Elinvar effect, maintaining an almost constant elastic modulus from 298 to 900 K (Fig.  1 a) [ 13 ]. Unlike conventional magnetoelastic mechanisms, Co 25 Ni 25 (TiZrHf) 50  exhibits pronounced heterogeneous strain fields arising from severe lattice distortion. These heterogeneous strain fields generate broad distributions of local bond stiffness and elastic energy [ 13 ]. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations further revealed that different strain components evolve oppositely with increasing temperature. Specifically, the average volumetric strain gradually increases because of thermal expansion, which enlarges the lattice constant and weakens interatomic bonding, thereby contributing to conventional thermoelastic softening. In contrast, the average von Mises strain continuously decreases with temperature, indicating progressive relaxation of local shear distortion and reduced structural disorder. This reduction in lattice disorder promotes a more ordered local atomic packing and increases bond stiffness, providing an additional modulus hardening contribution. When the softening effect induced by volumetric expansion is nearly balanced by the hardening effect associated with reduced lattice distortion, the overall elastic modulus becomes nearly temperature-independent, giving rise to the Elinvar effect (Fig.  1 b–d) [ 53 ,  54 – 55 ]. This mechanism also suggests that lattice distortion can progressively retard thermoelastic softening in HEAs. Since the degree of lattice distortion varies among different HEA systems depending on composition and local chemical complexity, the extent of elastic modulus degradation with temperature also differs accordingly. In general, larger lattice distortion leads to stronger distortion induced hardening and thus more effectively suppresses modulus softening [ 56 ]. Unlike transformation induced Elinvar systems, where modulus stabilization is associated with discrete phase transitions, the compensation mechanism in distorted HEAs is continuous and highly reversible, leading to improved thermal stability and reduced hysteresis [ 13 ]. Similar phenomena have also been observed in Fe-doped Co 25 Ni 25 (TiZrHf) 50  and CoNiTiZr HEAs [ 15 ,  57  ]. Similar distortion-mediated Elinvar behavior has also been reported in strain glass HEAs and highly distorted ceramic systems, further highlighting the universality of lattice distortion-driven thermoelastic stabilization. Zhang et al. observed a pronounced Elinvar effect in Ti 33 Nb 15 Zr 25 Hf 25 O 2  HEA accompanied by a strain glass transition [ 58 ]. Unlike conventional martensitic alloys with long-range transformation ordering, the alloy exhibited frozen nanoscale transformation domains and diffuse structural instability, which effectively suppressed abrupt modulus variation during thermal cycling [ 58 ]. The presence of local lattice variations and global structural stability enabled a broad temperature window with nearly constant elastic modulus, suggesting that strain glass-like states provide an effective pathway for achieving reversible Elinvar behavior in chemically complex alloys. A similar mechanism has also been identified in ceramic systems. Hu et al. reported an Elinvar-like effect in highly distorted Zr 6 Ta 2 O 17  ceramics, where severe lattice distortion and local structural heterogeneity generated anomalous thermoelastic behavior [ 14 ]. The authors proposed that the relaxation of distorted polyhedral structures at elevated temperatures could compensate for intrinsic thermoelastic softening, resulting in nearly temperature independent elastic modulus [ 14 ].

sections.heading: Non-hysteretic superelasticity
paragraphs: Superelasticity refers to the ability of materials to recover exceptionally large strains upon unloading, far beyond the elastic limit of conventional crystalline metals [ 16 ,  59 ]. To better distinguish different elastic deformation regimes, true linear elasticity describes fully reversible deformation following Hooke’s law, where stress is proportional to strain and the elastic modulus remains constant. In contrast, nonlinear elasticity refers to reversible deformation with a strain dependent elastic modulus. Pseudoelasticity generally involves recoverable deformation associated with reversible internal structural rearrangements or phase transformations and is often accompanied by mechanical hysteresis. Superelasticity can be regarded as a special form of pseudoelasticity, characterized by exceptionally large recoverable strain, typically enabled by stress-induced martensitic transformation. In traditional SMAs, superelasticity arises from reversible stress-induced martensitic transformations, where the parent phase transforms into martensite during loading and reverses upon unloading [ 18 ,  60 ]. Although such transformation-mediated mechanisms can generate recoverable strains exceeding several percent, they are usually accompanied by pronounced mechanical hysteresis and energy dissipation due to the frictional motion of transformation interfaces and irreversible defect accumulation [ 18 ,  60 ]. The intrinsic hysteresis of first-order martensitic transformations not only reduces energy storage efficiency, but also limits the applicability of superelastic materials in precision actuation and high frequency mechanical systems [ 18 ]. Therefore, achieving large recoverable strain together with minimal hysteresis remains a major challenge in the development of ultraelastic materials.

Recent studies have demonstrated that lattice distortion and structural heterogeneity in chemically complex alloys provide a fundamentally different route for realizing non-hysteretic superelasticity [ 13 ,  61 ,  62 ]. Unlike conventional SMAs, where recoverable strain originates from abrupt phase transformations, distorted HEAs can accommodate large elastic deformation through high lattice frictional stress and low elastic modulus. The severe atomic size mismatch and chemical disorder in HEAs generate heterogeneous strain fields and frustrated elastic strain energy landscape, which increases the Peierls barrier of dislocation gliding [ 13 ,  63 ,  64 ]. A representative example is the highly distorted Co 25 Ni 25 (HfTiZr) 50  high-entropy intermetallic reported by He et al. [ 13 ], which exhibits substantial intrinsic lattice distortion while maintaining a single phase B2 structure. Atomic-scale characterization and first-principles calculations revealed broad distributions of volumetric strain and shear strain, with the average von Mises strain approaching ~ 9% [ 13 ]. Such severe lattice distortion produces highly heterogeneous local atomic environments and a rugged energy landscape containing multiple metastable configurations, thereby enabling large reversible elastic deformation without triggering conventional martensitic transformation [ 13 ]. Importantly, the highly distorted Co 25 Ni 25 (HfTiZr) 50  alloy exhibits an elastic strain limit approaching ~ 2%, which is significantly higher than that of conventional crystalline alloys (Fig.  2 a, b) [ 13 ]. As demonstrated in Fig.  2 c, the rebound height of the steel ball on the Co 25 Ni 25 (HfTiZr) 50  alloy outperformed other superelastic materials [ 13 ]. At the same time, the alloy shows extremely low internal friction (tan δ  < 2 × 10 −4 ), indicating minimal mechanical energy dissipation during cyclic deformation [ 13 ]. Figure 2 a  Stress–strain curves of Co 25 Ni 25 (HfTiZr) 50  alloys exhibiting 2% linear elastic strain limit.  b  The comparison of elastic strain limit of Co 25 Ni 25 (HfTiZr) 50  and other conventional alloys.  c  A demonstration of superelasticity of Co 25 Ni 25 (HfTiZr) 50  with other alloys. Reproduced with permission from Ref. [ 13 ]. Copyright 2022, Springer Nature.

A similar concept of non-hysteretic superelasticity has also been demonstrated in Ni 55-x Co x Fe 18 Ga 27  chemically complex alloys [ 29 ]. By tuning Co concentration and short range ordering, the alloy gradually evolves from conventional martensitic superelasticity with pronounced hysteresis to a non-hysteretic stress–strain response [ 29 ]. The optimized Ni 35 Co 20 Fe 18 Ga 27  alloy exhibits ultra large recoverable strain up to 15.2% together with excellent cyclic stability over more than 8000 loading–unloading cycles [ 29 ]. In situ synchrotron diffraction revealed that the superelasticity is associated with continuous lattice parameter evolution and structural fluctuation rather than abrupt first order martensitic transformation [ 29 ]. Furthermore, neutron diffraction and electron microscopy observations demonstrated the existence of an atomic-scale entanglement of chemical ordering and lattice strains, which effectively smooths the energy landscape and suppresses transformation hysteresis [ 29 ].

The above results regarding non-hysteretic superelasticity in HEAs indicate that lattice distortion can fundamentally change the deformation mode of metallic materials. In conventional alloys, the elastic strain limit is usually restricted by early dislocation activities and/or irreversible plastic deformation [ 35 ]. However, in heavily distorted HEAs, heterogeneous strain fields increase lattice resistance to dislocation motion and stabilize reversible local lattice instability [ 63 ]. As a result, the elastic deformation regime can be substantially expanded, enabling continuous transitions from linear Hookean elasticity to nonlinear ultraelastic responses [ 13 ,  29  ]. This distortion-mediated mechanism provides a new physical framework for designing ultraelastic materials beyond conventional martensitic transformation theories.

sections.heading: Tuning superelasticity from Hookean to non-Hookean
paragraphs: As discussed above, lattice distortion in HEAs not only enhances the elastic strain limit, but also modifies the mode of elastic deformation. In conventional crystalline metals, elastic deformation generally follows Hooke’s law, where stress increases linearly with strain and the elastic modulus remains nearly constant within the elastic regime [ 65 ,  66 ]. Such Hookean elasticity originates from harmonic atomic bonding and reversible lattice stretching around equilibrium positions [ 35 ]. In contrast, many metastable alloys exhibit nonlinear elastic responses during deformation, where the elastic modulus evolves continuously with strain [ 18 ,  60 ]. This behavior, commonly referred to as non-Hookean superelasticity, is typically associated with stress-induced lattice instability or martensitic transformation [ 18 ,  60  ]. In traditional SMAs, non-Hookean superelasticity usually originates from stress-induced martensitic transformation [ 60 ]. During loading, the parent phase progressively transforms into martensite, producing nonlinear stress–strain behavior. However, because the transformation involves interface migration and first order phase transition, the deformation process is often associated with large hysteresis and irreversible energy dissipation.

Alternatively, recent studies indicate that lattice distortion in HEAs provides a new pathway for continuously tuning superelasticity from Hookean to non-Hookean regimes by regulating lattice instability and martensitic transformation behavior [ 13 ,  28  ]. A representative example is the B2 structured (TiZrHf) 50 Ni 50-x Co x  alloy system, where the elastic response evolves systematically with increasing Co concentration (Fig.  3 a, b) [ 28 ]. At relatively low Co contents, the alloy exhibits nearly linear Hookean elasticity with a stable B2 parent phase. With increasing Co concentration, however, the stress–strain behavior gradually changes into pronounced nonlinear superelasticity accompanied by recoverable transformation strain. Interestingly, further increasing Co content restores a nearly linear elastic response again, indicating a reversible transition between Hookean and non-Hookean deformation modes. Micropillar compression experiments further revealed strong orientation dependence of the nonlinear superelastic behavior in (TiZrHf) 50 Ni 28 Co 22  alloys (Fig.  3 c, d) [ 28 ]. Under specific crystallographic orientations, the alloy exhibited highly reversible nonlinear deformation with minimal residual strain after repeated loading unloading cycles. Such behavior suggests that lattice distortion not only modifies the overall transformation stability, but also influences local strain accommodation pathways and directional lattice instability. Crystallographic orientation further plays an important role because different loading directions activate distinct transformation pathways through orientation-dependent resolved shear stresses. The coexistence of chemically induced local strain heterogeneity and crystallographic anisotropy therefore critically governs the transition between Hookean and non-Hookean elasticity. Figure 3 a  Macroscopic stress–strain curves of (TiZrHf) 50 Ni 50-x Co x  alloys showing transitions from linear to nonlinear and back to linear elasticity with increasing Co contents.  b  Cyclic loading–unloading curves of (TiZrHf) 50 Ni 50-x Co x  alloys.  c  Orientation dependent micropillar compression stress–strain curves of (TiZrHf) 50 Ni 28 Co 22  alloy.  d  Cyclic micropillar compression of (TiZrHf) 50 Ni 28 Co 22  alloy in [011] directions [ 28 ].

This unusual evolution originates from the strong coupling among lattice distortion, composition-dependent electronic structure, and martensitic transformation stability. In the (TiZrHf) 50 Ni 50-x Co x  system, Co substitution not only modifies the local lattice strain state but also changes the electron localization and local chemical bonding environment, thereby altering the energy difference between the B2 parent phase and martensitic structures [ 28 ]. Such compositional tuning directly affects phase stability and the martensitic transformation temperature. When the transformation temperature approaches the testing temperature, the alloy enters a metastable regime in which stress-induced transformation becomes energetically favorable, promoting nonlinear superelastic deformation. As illustrated in Fig.  4 a, b, both the von Mises strain and volumetric strain evolve sensitively with Ni/Co ratio, indicating substantial changes in local lattice distortion and structural instability. At intermediate Co concentrations, the alloy approaches a metastable state where the energy barrier for martensitic transformation becomes sufficiently low to allow stress-induced lattice instability during deformation [ 28 ]. Consequently, the alloy exhibits continuous nonlinear elastic deformation and large recoverable strain. In contrast to conventional SMAs with abrupt martensitic interface motion, the transformation in these chemically complex alloys becomes spatially diffuse due to severe lattice distortion and heterogeneous local strain fields [ 19 ,  28  ]. Figure 4 a  Von Mises strain and  b  volumetric strain for B2 and B19 structures with different Ni:Co ratio in (TiZrHf) 50 Ni 50-x Co x  alloys.  c  The schematic of lattice strain evolution and hidden strain order governing Hookean versus non-Hookean superelasticity [ 28 ].

Here, the hidden strain order does not refer to conventional structural ordering or long-range crystallographic symmetry breaking. Instead, it describes a composition-dependent competitive strain evolution between the B2 parent phase and the B19’ martensitic phase. With increasing Co content, the lattice strain associated with the B2 phase gradually decreases, whereas that associated with the competing B19’ phase progressively increases (Fig.  4 c) [ 28 ]. This opposite strain evolution establishes a competitive relationship between the two phases and strongly influences their relative stability. As a result, although only one apparent phase structure may be experimentally observed under equilibrium conditions, the strain state associated with the competing phase remains implicitly embedded in the system and continues to affect phase transformation behavior. This hidden strain competition continuously modifies the Gibbs free energy balance between the B2 and B19’ phases and thereby regulates martensitic transformation stability. From a microscopic perspective, the transition from Hookean to non-Hookean superelasticity is governed by this evolution of lattice distortion and the resulting change in relative phase stability. At low Co contents, the highly distorted B2 phase remains relatively unstable, favoring linear Hookean elasticity dominated by homogeneous lattice stretching. With increasing Co concentration, the reduction of strain in the B2 phase together with the enhanced strain in the B19’ phase lowers the transformation barrier and promotes stress-induced lattice instability, leading to nonlinear non-Hookean superelasticity accompanied by reversible transformation strain [ 28 ]. Therefore, tuning Co concentration effectively adjusts the relative phase stability through lattice distortion engineering, enabling continuous modulation of elastic behavior from Hookean to non-Hookean regimes.

The ability to reversibly tailor superelasticity through lattice distortion provides new opportunities for designing programmable ultraelastic materials [ 28 ]. More importantly, these findings demonstrate that lattice distortion can act as an effective structural parameter for controlling the relative stability of competing phases and the associated deformation pathways in HEAs. By regulating the distortion state of parent and martensitic phases through compositional design, it becomes possible to continuously tune elastic responses ranging from stable Hookean elasticity to transformation assisted non-Hookean superelasticity. Such distortion engineering strategies may ultimately enable the development of next-generation ultraelastic materials with high elastic strain limits, low energy dissipation, and adaptive mechanical functionality.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: In summary, recent advances have demonstrated that lattice distortion plays a central role in enabling unconventional elastic anomalies in HEAs and other chemically complex materials. Severe lattice distortion and the resulting heterogeneous strain fields fundamentally modify elastic behavior, providing new mechanisms for achieving thermoelastic stability, large recoverable strain, and tunable superelasticity. For the Elinvar effect, lattice distortion can compensate conventional thermoelastic softening through the relaxation and evolution of heterogeneous local strain states, enabling a nearly temperature independent elastic modulus over broad temperature ranges. In addition, lattice distortion enhances elastic strain limits and modulates deformation modes, allowing continuous tuning of elastic behavior from conventional Hookean elasticity to transformation assisted non-Hookean superelasticity. Despite these exciting advances, several important scientific questions remain open. A major challenge is how to quantitatively design and predict lattice distortion using reliable structural characteristics, enabling more precise control of elastic responses. In addition, because lattice distortion is often strongly coupled with chemical short-range order, decoupling their respective contributions to elastic anomalies remains difficult. Further studies are also needed to clarify the fundamental relationship between local structural heterogeneity, phase stability, and deformation pathways across multiple length scales. From an application perspective, several limitations and challenges must also be addressed before these materials can be translated into practical components. The long-term stability of elastic anomalies under cyclic loading, fatigue, and service environments remains insufficiently understood. Moreover, maintaining distortion-controlled microstructures during large-scale processing and manufacturing presents additional challenges. Future progress will require the integration of advanced characterization, multiscale modeling, and alloy design strategies to better understand and engineer lattice distortion. Such efforts may ultimately enable the development of next-generation ultraelastic materials with programmable elastic responses, low energy dissipation, and robust thermoelastic stability.
